# developer-tools

## make make Better

Everybody who gets fed up with Make ships a new task runner. [just](https://just.systems/), [Task](https://taskfile.dev/), and [run](https://runtool.dev/) each throw out the Makefile and invent a [justfile](https://just.systems/man/en/quick-start.html), a [Taskfile.yml](https://taskfile.dev/docs/reference/schema), or a [Runfile](https://runtool.dev/docs/runfile-syntax.html) to replace it, and each has a crowd cheering it on.

I have [previously argued](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html) that the behaviors people hate about Make are Chesterton's Fences that should not be torn down. The *fair* complaints are a different set, and they are all about what it's like to *use* `make`: asking it for help, typing it bare, looking at what it's about to do.

None of these are about anything you wrote in your `Makefile`; every one lives in the `make` binary. Upstream GNU Make hasn't shipped a release since 4.4.1 in February 2023, and macOS still ships GNU Make 3.81 from 2006.

Keep the Makefile, keep every fence intact, and improve the program that reads it:

Let's **make `make` better**.

## What's Actually Broken in the Binary

### `make --help` Belongs to Make

Ask `make --help` and the binary answers about itself. GNU Make intercepts the flag before reading a line of your `Makefile` and prints its own option table, a feature dating to 1993.[^help-1993] `make test --help` ignores `test` and prints the same help text as before.

Ask `make help` instead and you are running a target. If the project's author wrote one called `help`, you get whatever they made it print. If they didn't:

```text
make: *** No rule to make target 'help'.  Stop.
```

So there are two things to ask about - the binary and the project - and Make has a contract for only one of them. No released version of GNU Make can list a project's targets; the development branch gained `--print-targets` in January 2024,[^print-targets-commit] which prints names only, and it still hasn't shipped.

The workaround is [five pasted lines](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#five-lines-beat-a-new-binary), and it is still a workaround. Copying it into every repository has been called [the Makefile Effect](https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/01/10/Be-aware-of-the-Makefile-effect): When a tool is "too complicated (or annoying) to use from scratch", people stop writing its files and start copying templates. Thibaud Chupin [said the same](https://thibaud.space/2026/10/the-case-against-makefiles.html) of Make's workarounds: "You just have to remember to copy them into every new project you do." 

Alas, no copy/pasted magic target can rescue `make --help` while the binary swallows the flag first.

In the session logs from my own three workstations, AI coding agents reached for a dashed help flag (`--help` or `-h`) in [92.7% of 1,042 help calls](/garden/cli-help-patterns.html#preliminary-field-data-from-stockroom), and a `make help`-style verb in only 2.2%. An agent following that 92.7% instinct in a Make repository gets Make's 1993 option table instead of your targets.

How to build a project is absolutely the build tool's question to answer - it surely knows! And while perhaps `make --help` should still answer about Make, there also must needs be a standard way to interrogate the project's own targets.

It is the binary's job to make that happen.

### Keystroke Savers from 1976

Two more warts date from an era when saving keystrokes on a slow terminal was worth a little magic, and nearly every Unix build compiled C. Or something like it. Or at least *compiled files.*

First, running bare `make` with no arguments executes whichever ordinary target happens to sit at the top of the Makefile - or at the top of the first file an `include` pulls in above it, which is why GNU Make had to add `.DEFAULT_GOAL` to wrestle control back. Saving four keystrokes over `make build` made sense in 1976.

Typing a bare command in an unfamiliar repository shouldn't kick off a mystery build. It should print some useful guidance and exit.

Second, GNU Make 4.4.1 still ships with 92 built-in implicit rules baked into the binary:[^other-makes-builtins] recipes for C, C++, Fortran, Pascal, Modula-2 (`.mod`), Ratfor (`.r`), TeX, and CWEB, plus rules for checking missing files straight out of RCS (`%,v`) and SCCS (`SCCS/s.%`). Back when almost every project compiled `.c` files into `.o` files, built-in recipes meant a tiny Makefile worked out of the box. Today Make orchestrates `pytest`, `cargo`, `docker`, and plenty else, and those 92 ghost rules only clutter debug traces and misfire when a filename matches one. Even `MAKEFLAGS += --no-builtin-rules` only started clearing them inside a Makefile in [GNU Make 4.0][make-news] (2013), so on macOS's stock 3.81 a Makefile can't even turn them all off by itself.

Those rules did their work back when nearly every build was C. A Make for 2026 should ship none of them.

### Make Keeps the Graph to Itself

A real graph - say, nine targets in three parallel tracks, three deep - is hard to see when its edges are scattered across nine rule definitions in a flat file read top-to-bottom.

GNU Make has no graph view of its own. [Requests to export the graph](https://web.archive.org/web/20251017115001/http://savannah.gnu.org/bugs/?25751) go back to 2009, and add-ons such as [makefile2graph](https://github.com/lindenb/makefile2graph) have to scrape Make's debug output to draw one.

The binary already builds the graph. It should print it like a proper Unix program.[^unix-philosophy]

### Nothing Enforces the Verbs

`make test` is only a convention. The GNU Coding Standards [say flat-out](https://web.archive.org/web/20261030235037/https://www.gnu.org/prep/standards/html_node/Standard-Targets.html): "All GNU programs should have the following targets in their Makefiles:" and list `all`, `install`, `clean`, `check`, and more. The Automake manual [sums up the result](https://web.archive.org/web/20261029155032/https://www.gnu.org/software/automake/manual/html_node/GNU-Build-System.html): "A unified build system that makes all packages almost indistinguishable by the installer." Nothing in Make itself enforces this, though, so one repository has `make check`, the next has `make test`, and a third invents `make test-ci`.

Nobody can guess the right name without a standard, and standards hold best when the build tool enforces them.

Maven started enforcing them in October 2005. At the time, its 1.0 release had let projects script their builds in a `maven.xml` file written in [Jelly](https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-jelly/), an XML scripting language. Maven 2.0 [deleted](https://svn.apache.org/repos/infra/websites/production/maven/content/maven1.html) `maven.xml` and replaced it with a fixed lifecycle: `validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install`, `deploy`. Plugins bind their goals to those phases, projects configure the plugins in a declarative `pom.xml`, and the logic lives in prepackaged plugins, each of which has passed its own test suite. Maven's [lifecycle guide](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-lifecycle.html) states the contract beautifully:

> For the person building a project, this means that it is only necessary to learn a small set of commands to build any Maven project, and the POM will ensure they get the results they desired.

A fixed lifecycle also answers most of the help question before anyone asks it. Nobody runs `mvn validate --help`: you know what `validate` is for before you clone the repository, and the `pom.xml` is the canonical, inspectable definition of what `validate` will do *here.*

Gradle took the opposite bet, turning the build file into a Groovy or Kotlin program - [an application in the delivery pipeline](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#its-just-no-place-to-run-an-application) - and lost.

Gradle's own documentation [now says](https://docs.gradle.org/8.2/userguide/authoring_maintainable_build_scripts.html) "The end goal of every build script should be to only contain declarative language elements", and since 2023 it has been building [Declarative Gradle](https://blog.gradle.org/declarative-gradle), where "Generic control flow and calls to arbitrary methods will be disallowed" and logic moves into plugins.

While the `make`, `just`, and `run` camps argue about what commands a repository should even have, Gradle's re-deriving from first principles what Maven's known for over two decades.

Maybe one project in ten thousand truly doesn't fit a standard lifecycle like Maven's. Before you decide yours is that one, ask who knows more about software lifecycles: the Apache Software Foundation, with twenty years of other people's builds behind it, or you and your new project.

> If you don’t see the use of Maven's lifecycle phases, I certainly won’t let you work around them. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of them, I may allow you to create your own.

A better Make should reserve a short list of lifecycle verbs as tasks (not file targets) and hold every project to them. Maven-style.

### Timestamps Don't Travel

In 1976, using the filesystem's own timestamps as the build's cache key was a brilliant zero-storage trick. GNU Make's maintainer, Paul D. Smith, [described it in 2003](https://web.archive.org/web/20241018034053/https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-make/2003-03/msg00004.html): "Currently make is completely stateless, because we only compare relative timestamps between files". The same message calls content hashing "an absolute must-have if make is to survive too much into the future".

Take a file target:

```makefile
SRCS := main.py requirements.txt

function.zip: $(SRCS)
	rm -f $@
	zip -q $@ $(SRCS)
```

Make can only skip building `function.zip` when an earlier run left `function.zip` on disk with a newer timestamp than `main.py`. A fresh CI runner starts with a clean disk, so nothing gets skipped. Restore yesterday's `function.zip` from a CI cache and `git checkout` still trips you up: it stamps every source file with the current time rather than when the file last changed, so `main.py` looks newer than the cached zip and Make rebuilds it anyway.

Meanwhile, [GitHub says](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching) it "will remove any cache entries that have not been accessed in over 7 days" so a slow project will eventually repeat work even if none of its inputs change *and* the cache keys are perfect.

Further complicating matters, Make never notices when the recipe line itself changes in the Makefile: you've got to pay attention with the right incantation or just re-run the whole build lest ye be left with needed work uncompleted.

What build state should travel between machines, and what should the tool do when that state is missing, stale, or evicted? Nobody has a good answer yet, which figures: cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in computer science.[^two-hard-things] Caching alone can't be the whole answer, either, because it tempts developers to count on cache hits to keep work from repeating - which holds only until the cache is evicted.

A better Make should consider file contents and recipe text instead of clocks, and clearly specify what it does on an invalidated *or missing* "cache" entry.

## Twenty-Six Tools and Still No Successor

Evan Martin, who wrote Ninja, admits in the retrospective ["The Success and Failure of Ninja"](https://neugierig.org/software/blog/2020/05/ninja.html): "I regret not spending more time researching before building".

So before proposing another tool, I went looking for the one I want across 26 build and task runners, from Plan 9's [mk](https://9fans.github.io/plan9port/man/man1/mk.html) to this year's crop of hotshot upstarts. Nobody has built it. What I found instead is strangers rebuilding the fences from ["just run make"](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html), each for a different reason than mine:

- [Ninja](https://ninja-build.org/) refused build-time options, for speed.[^ninja-options] That is [the no-flags fence](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#targets-take-no-flags).
- [makesure](https://github.com/xonixx/makesure) refused task arguments, to keep the build file self-contained.[^makesure-arguments] Same fence.
- [tup](https://gittup.org/tup/) refused alternate build modes, for usability.[^tup-modes] Same fence again.
- [Bazel](https://bazel.build/)'s Starlark language refused `while` loops, to keep build code simple.[^starlark-loops] That is the fence against [running an application in your build](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#its-just-no-place-to-run-an-application).
- [Maven](https://maven.apache.org/) froze its lifecycle verbs back in 2.0, so that one small set of commands builds any project. That is the no-flags fence built one rail higher: Make refuses flags on a verb, and Maven fixes the verbs themselves. Both guard [commands every caller can guess](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#targets-take-no-flags).
- Et cetera, et cetera.[^more-fences]

The nearest thing to the shape I want is [remake](https://github.com/Trepan-Debuggers/remake), which "patched GNU Make 4.3 sources to add improved error reporting, tracing, target listing, graph visualization, profiling, and more." It proves that target listing and a graph view fit inside a binary that reads ordinary Makefiles. It is also a fork whose last release was in January 2022, and its target list waits behind a `--tasks` flag of its own that an agent has no reason to try.

Native Windows is the other gap. Make isn't pre-installed there and most Makefiles assume a POSIX shell, so for a developer who just happens to sit at a Windows workstation my answer is WSL or a [devcontainer](https://containers.dev/). A project that is Windows all the way down deserves better than that, and that's something else that a better Make could address.[^native-windows]

## A Make That Reads Your Makefile

Every fix lives in the binary, so a successor should be an improved binary that reads the Makefiles people already have. It keeps all five fences:

1. [Targets that can be files *or* tasks](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#a-target-is-a-file-until-you-say-otherwise)
2. [Prerequisites in no promised order](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#siblings-run-in-any-order)
3. [Targets that take no flags](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#targets-take-no-flags)
4. [A fresh shell for every recipe line](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#every-line-gets-its-own-shell)
5. [A language you don't program in](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#its-just-no-place-to-run-an-application)

What changes in the binary is the rest:

1. **Help and bare invocation:** there is one standard way to ask the binary for the project's own targets, wherever `make --help` itself ends up pointing, and a bare `make` prints guidance and exits without running anything.
2. **No 1976 ghost rules:** the 92 built-in implicit rules are gone.
3. **Graph inspection:** the binary prints the dependency graph it already builds, in a form other programs can read.
4. **Reserved lifecycle verbs:** how does it tell a task from a file without `.PHONY`? That's the neat part: you never tell it anything. **Reserve the lifecycle names**, Maven-style. A reserved name (`build`, `test`, `package`, `deploy`, `clean`, and friends) is always a task that no cache skips, and any other name is a file on disk - giving Make Maven's universal verb contract without Maven's XML plugin plumbing. Need a task with a different name? `.PHONY:` still works, and we could even add a clearer alias for the 21st century.
5. **Change detection without clocks:** file contents and recipe text decide what is stale, and the binary clearly specifies what it does when its saved state is invalidated or missing.
6. **The host's own shell on Windows:** a Windows build of the binary sends each recipe line to `cmd.exe` or PowerShell, the way a Unix build sends it to `sh`, and that port gets tested like the others.

### Must We Keep Makefiles?

[Yes.](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#must-we-keep-makefiles)

---

A returning reader has caught me by now: I've [argued](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#five-lines-beat-a-new-binary) that saving five lines of Makefile isn't worth deploying a new binary everywhere, and here I am asking for a new binary. Price the two trades side by side:

Moving to `just` or `run` costs a new binary on every machine before anyone can run a single task, a rewrite of every build file, **and the fences.** Nobody prices that last part until they're stuck maintaining an [untested glue ghetto](/2026/11/13/just-run-make.html#its-just-no-place-to-run-an-application) in their build tool. 

Our *better Make* binary reads the Makefiles you already have. Modern repositories keep working on day one without a rewrite[^day-one-compat] - even alongside machines still running stock `make` - and work *better* everywhere the new binary lands.

Best case, GNU Make sands its own edges and this tool never needs to exist.

But I've waited more than a decade for that while everyone else shipped tools that tear the fences down, so I might build the one that keeps them myself, if a reader convinced by this post doesn't beat me to it.

Keep your Makefiles. **make make better**.

---

## Footnotes & References

[^help-1993]: GNU Make's [NEWS][make-news] entry for version 3.63, dated 22 Jan 1993: "Make now accepts long options. There is now an informative usage message that tells you what all the options are and what they do."

[^print-targets-commit]: Paul D. Smith's [commit](https://web.archive.org/web/20240429135352/https://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/make.git/commit/?id=31036e648f4a92ae0cce215eb3d60a1311a09c60) of 8 January 2024: "Add an option to print a list of targets defined in the makefiles." GNU Make 4.4.1, still the latest release, came out in February 2023.

[^more-fences]: The list goes on. Two more, if you want to match them to their fences yourself: [Hume's paper on mk][mk-paper] says "Mk does not define the order of execution of independent recipes." [werk](https://github.com/simonask/werk)'s README says "`werk` will never be a scripting language."


[^other-makes-builtins]: GNU Make has company. POSIX [requires](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/make.html#tag_20_76_13_09) a default rule set for C, lex, yacc, and shell scripts, and records that its authors debated dropping it: "They provide convenience, but do not enhance portability of applications." OpenBSD's [mk](https://github.com/openbsd/src/blob/master/share/mk/sys.mk) carries 40 suffix rules for C, C++, Fortran, Ratfor, Pascal, assembler, lex, yacc, and shell scripts. Microsoft's NMAKE has [predefined rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/reference/predefined-rules) too, and an `/R` switch to ignore them. Two tools already ship none. "Unlike make, mk has no built-in rules", says [Hume's paper on mk][mk-paper], and Ninja's [manual](https://ninja-build.org/manual.html) lists them among its non-goals: "Out of the box, Ninja has no rules for e.g. compiling C code."

[^unix-philosophy]: The [Unix philosophy](https://cscie2x.dce.harvard.edu/hw/ch01s06.html) is to build small, simple tools that do one thing well and compose them into larger systems. Here in particular, I mean: *"Design programs to be connected to other programs."*

[mk-paper]: https://9p.io/sys/doc/mk.html

[^two-hard-things]: "There are 2 hard problems in computer science: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-1 errors." <https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TwoHardThings.html>

[^ninja-options]: Ninja's [manual](https://ninja-build.org/manual.html#:~:text=Options%20belong%20in%20the%20program%20that%20generates%20the%20ninja%20files) lists "build-time customization of the build" among the things it deliberately leaves out: "Options belong in the program that generates the ninja files."


[^makesure-arguments]: Under "Omitted features" in makesure's [README](https://github.com/xonixx/makesure#omitted-features): "We deliberately don't support this feature. The idea is that the build file should be self-contained, so have all the information to run in it, no external arguments should be required."


[^tup-modes]: Rule 3 on page 7 of Mike Shal's 2009 paper, ["Build System Rules and Algorithms"](https://gittup.org/tup/build_system_rules_and_algorithms.pdf): "Usability: There must not be different ways of building the system that the user must remember in order to accommodate rules 1) or 2)."

[^starlark-loops]: Under "No unbounded loops" in Starlark's [design notes](https://github.com/bazelbuild/starlark/blob/master/design.md#no-unbounded-loops): "Support for unbounded loops (e.g. `while`) would encourage users to write more complex code."

[^native-windows]: Nothing in the fences requires POSIX. The shell fence is a fresh shell for every line and copy-paste parity with *your* terminal, and on Windows your terminal is `cmd.exe` or PowerShell.

	GNU Make's Windows port already gets halfway. Its [README](https://web.archive.org/web/20261113011611/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mirror/make/4.4.1/README.W32) says that on a system with no Bourne shell, "All command lines will be put into batch files and executed via $(COMSPEC)", and admits that this style of execution "has not been tested that carefully". The mechanism is there; what's missing is the testing.

	A Makefile full of `cmd.exe` recipes won't run on Linux, but neither will the project it builds. And if you really need that, well, CMake can [generate platform-specific Makefiles](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-generators.7.html) for you...


[^day-one-compat]: What breaks are the 1976 holdovers this post drops on purpose: `./configure && make` scripts expecting bare `make` to run the first target, C builds leaning on the 92 implicit rules, and any Makefile where a reserved verb like `build` or `test` named an actual file on disk. None of those are the repositories people are fleeing for `just` or `run`.

[make-news]: https://web.archive.org/web/20241213073812/http://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/make.git/tree/NEWS

## Worktrees, Baby

Git's known how to do this for *years*!

## The Object Database Is the Whole Trick

Linus Torvalds's [first README](https://github.com/git/git/blob/e83c5163316f89bfbde7d9ab23ca2e25604af290/README), April 2005, splits Git into two abstractions.

> There are two object abstractions: the "object database", and the "current directory cache".

Under the heading for the database, the same file says:

> The object database is literally just a content-addressable collection of objects.

The cache is the checkout you are looking at: names, permissions, and blobs. History lives in the database. Another folder can point at the same database, hold a different cache, and show a different branch. Both folders read the same objects.

```mermaid
graph TD
    classDef store fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#7b1fa2,color:#000
    classDef tree fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#01579b,color:#000
    Store["Object database"]:::store --> Main["Main checkout"]:::tree
    Store --> Fix["Checkout for fix-login"]:::tree
    Store --> Agent["Checkout for an agent"]:::tree
```

The second folder took longer than the idea.

In March 2007 Julian Phillips checked in `contrib/workdir/git-new-workdir`, a script that symlinks `objects`, `refs`, and `config` into a new directory. He was writing down a habit Junio Hamano already had. The [commit message](https://github.com/git/git/commit/4f01748d51b530c297eeb5a0ece9af923d5db937) carries Junio's caveat whole:

> This risks confusion for an uninitiated if you update a ref that is checked out in another working tree, but modulo that caveat it works reasonably well.

One branch, two directories, and a shared `refs`. Move the branch in one directory and the other directory is standing on a ref that just left.

[Git 2.5.0](https://github.blog/open-source/git/git-2-5-including-multiple-worktrees-and-triangular-workflows/), released 29 July 2015, gave the second checkout its command. Linked worktrees were already in Git by then, doing the job of that symlink script. Nguyễn Thái Ngọc Duy introduced `git worktree` and Eric Sunshine added `git worktree add`, which gives a linked worktree its own `HEAD` and its own index.[^revnews] Git refuses to check out a branch that another worktree already has.[^worktree] The release announcement still called the feature experimental, and `git worktree add` still wanted a path of your choosing. Removing the worktree meant remembering that path. I stayed in one checkout. The agent stayed there with me.

## The Path Was the Tax

`git worktree` will make the second checkout, and then it will ask you where to put it. I built `git wt` so I would stop answering. It lives in [git-aliases](https://github.com/Texarkanine/git-aliases), my collection of small Git utilities.

`git wt go` is the way in, and it is idempotent. You name a branch and land in a worktree whose path comes from the repository and that branch. Name the branch again and you get the same folder. The second run changes nothing.

```
~/worktrees/<owner>/<repo>/<repo>-<branch>
```

`git@github.com:octocat/Hello-World.git` on `fix-login` is `~/worktrees/octocat/Hello-World/Hello-World-fix-login`. A slash in the branch name adds a directory level, so `feature/login` becomes `Hello-World-feature/login`. A branch that does not exist yet is created from the commit you are on.

`git wt done` is the way out. The folder is deleted. The branch and the commits stay, so you can throw the directory away. Uncommitted work stops the command. Ignored files go with the directory: a `.env` you never committed, and `node_modules`, leave with the folder. The main checkout, the clone you already had, stays.

`git wt cleanup` is the pile. Every worktree `go` made for this repository, one list, one question: delete it?. Clean ones go. Dirty ones stay. This means you don't have to check every one by hand to see if there's any real work left there.

Because they're *worktrees*, deleting the folder of a clean branch just means you can `git switch ...` to it later, because it's still in your clone's database - just not at that path on disk anymore.

By default it only cleans up *this repository's* worktrees, but `--all` lets you run that sweep for every repository under `~/worktrees`, from any directory.

The rest of the contract is in the [README](https://github.com/Texarkanine/git-aliases/blob/c7cd053/subcommands/git-wt/README.md#where-worktrees-go).

`git wt go` prints a path and leaves your shell where it is. You've still got to `cd` - no process can do that for you.

Well, there is one process that can - your shell! The `git-aliases` have optional shell support, which, when installed with `make shell`, installs a `wt` function for bash and zsh that wraps the helper and changes directory for you. Now you just `wt go <branch>` or `wt done` and it works. Scripts can call `git wt` and `cd` (or perform other necessary operations) on the printed path.

## Cursor's Clock

`git wt cleanup` sees the worktrees you made with `git wt go`. Cursor makes its own worktrees, and it deletes them on another schedule.

Ask in the [IDE](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees) with `/worktree`, or on the [command line](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/using) with `agent --worktree`, and the checkout lands under `~/.cursor/worktrees`. Since Cursor 3.5 the editor deletes older entries once the machine passes a documented cap of 25.[^cursorcap]

![Is 25 worktrees a lot?](is-25-worktrees-a-lot.jpg)

So *depending* on the situation, you might want to clean up Cursor's worktrees much sooner than Cursor would get around to it. You'd need to enumerate them all, check to see if each one had any uncommitted work left in it, and... hey, that sounds a lot like what we just built above!

`git wt cleanup +cursor` lumps Cursor's worktrees in with yours. Now you can easily clean up these potentially-languishing folders of potentially-large size!

## Type This

You need `git`, `bash`, and `~/.local/bin` on your `PATH`. `make` helps with the installation but isn't used to actually do the thing.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Texarkanine/git-aliases.git
cd git-aliases
make
make shell
```

Open a new shell so the function is loaded.

```bash
cd /path/to/your/repo
wt go fix-login
```

That puts you in the new folder, on `fix-login`. If the branch did not exist, it does now, forked from whatever you had checked out. Edit, commit, and push the way you already do.

```bash
wt done
git branch
```

You are back in the main checkout. `fix-login` is still in that list. `wt go fix-login` brings the folder back.

When a few of them have piled up:

```bash
wt cleanup --list
wt cleanup
wt cleanup +cursor --list
wt cleanup +cursor
```

Read the list... then answer the one question!

## A Lock Is a Lock

`+cursor` had a pile I could find, so I wanted a `+claude` beside it. Same sweep, one more token.

The reason why that didn't work is instructive in reinforcing the reason to use `git wt` *instead* of either harness' own built-in worktree management!

[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees) can make the worktree for you. `claude --worktree feature-auth` puts it inside the repository, at `.claude/worktrees/feature-auth/`, on a branch named `worktree-feature-auth`. 

> The docs tell you to gitignore that directory, so those files stay out of `git status` in the main checkout.

Whaaat? Doesn't that sound like a colossal, looming footgun?

The location is a real limit. `cleanup --all` finds repositories by reading `~/worktrees`, and with `+cursor` by reading `~/.cursor/worktrees`. Claude's folders sit inside whichever clone you launched from. Once you are in that clone, `git worktree list` shows them. Finding **every clone on a machine** is a whole different ballgame. I could have shipped a flag that works only when you are already there - just don't support `--all` with `+claude`.

The lock is where that plan stopped.

While a session is running, Claude holds `git worktree lock` on the worktree, and `git worktree remove` will not remove a lock. A live session asked the directory to stay.

An interactive session's exit already cleans the worktree up after itself. An unnamed session with no changes is also cleaned up. A named session, or one that still has (uncommitted) work, asks you before it deletes anything. The worktrees that survive are ones that you *chose* to keep.

At least in the moment.

There are two ways that a Claude Code worktree might linger after you want it to:

1. a noninteractive session with a worktree - `claude -p --worktree` - that has since exited.
2. an interactive session you chose to keep, but have since changed your mind and forgotten about.

And, on disk, those will look indistinguishable from

1. a noninteractive session's worktree whose session is currently running.
2. an interactive session you chose to keep, *and still want*

We can't tell them apart, so we can't unlock and delete them.

Technically, Claude Code can tell the first one apart because the `git worktree lock` is a file with freeform text content, and Claude Code writes a sentence with a process id in it, which it parses on its own to check if the process is still running. We can't rely on that, as that is not a documented, public interface of Claude Code.

Technically, Cursor would have the same issue in a different flavor with its managed worktrees - it also periodically cleans up worktrees.

In both cases, the answer is simple: Make & manage the worktree yourself, and launch your harness in that directory:

```bash
wt go feature-auth
claude
```

You are already in `~/worktrees/.../<repo>-feature-auth`.

Now your harness "doesn't even" know it's using a worktree - at least, it certainly doesn't think it's supposed to manage them. You're using one tool to manage them both, and so if *you* `git wt done` when you're done, then you know that anything lingering is something you kept on purpose.

And if you're changing your mind and want to abandon some, `git wt cleanup --list --all` can list *all* of them, so you can decide which, if any, should be kept.

## I Used to Clone Into /tmp

You are on a branch, and the work is unfinished. A second task shows up, and it does not belong on this branch. Checking out the other branch means putting this one down: a stash, a commit you are not ready to make, or waiting until the first task is done.

I cloned the repository a second time. The clone often went in `/tmp`. Now the second task had a folder but each clone carried its own copy of the objects, and I had to remember which folder(s) I was allowed to throw away. And where they were!

A worktree from `git wt go` is that second folder without the second clone or detective work. The first branch stays checked out, dirty, where you left it. The second task gets its own checkout and its own branch. A third task gets a third. Six, if you have six tasks. They share one object database. Git refuses to check the same branch out in two of them, so each task sits on a branch of its own[^worktree]... you can't mess it up!

When the task is finished, `wt done` removes the folder and leaves the branch. The name is still there when you run `git branch`. The moment to notice is the itch to wait, or to clone into `/tmp`. That itch is a worktree waiting to sprout.

Once you have opened the second checkout yourself, you can tell an agent to take one instead of editing the branch you are standing on. Cursor's `/worktree` is that ask, as is Claude's own `--worktree`... resist the temptation! `git wt go` keeps your extra disk usage all in one discoverable place.

Worktrees. [Just try the thing!](/2026/08/01/just-try-the-thing.html).

---

## References

[^revnews]: Git Rev News, Edition 5, 8 July 2015. The linked-worktree facility had already landed, more than half a year earlier, to replace `contrib/git-new-workdir`. The same edition names Nguyễn Thái Ngọc Duy for the `git worktree` command and Eric Sunshine for `git worktree add`. Git 2.5.0 shipped on 29 July 2015. <https://git.github.io/rev_news/2015/07/08/edition-5/>
[^worktree]: Git documentation, git-worktree. Adding a worktree refuses a branch that is already checked out in another worktree. <https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree>
[^lockreason]: A locked Claude Code agent worktree whose reason string was `claude agent agent- (pid 197259)`, for a process that was no longer running. <https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/57765>
[^claudesweep]: Claude Code documentation, "Run parallel sessions with worktrees." Since v2.1.210 the sweep releases a lock Claude set for a session whose process has exited. <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees>
[^cursorcap]: Cursor documentation, "Worktrees," section "Worktrees cleanup," describing Cursor 3.5 and later. The default `cursor.worktreeMaxCount` is 25 per machine. The settings example sets `cursor.worktreeCleanupIntervalHours` to 6. <https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees>

## Steal These Status Lines

I want the model, the context window, and the burn rate all on the same row, right below the prompt. [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/) and the [Cursor CLI](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/overview) both do that the same way: they run a command, pipe session JSON to stdin, and render stdout as a [status line](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline). Plenty of people have one. These are the ones I actually look at, on a Mac and on Linux ([WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/)).

The shared row is the same in both harnesses: the model name, a fifteen-cell context bar that runs green to red, an emoji that flips at 20 / 70 / 90 percent (🟢 ⚡ 🔥 🚨), and the repo plus branch when you are in a git tree.

Claude then adds what its payload already has: session cost in dollars, a five-hour rate bar, a seven-day rate bar.

Cursor does not ship session dollars in the status-line payload or the usage API, so that slot is empty on purpose. In its place I pull first-party ([Grok](https://cursor.com/docs/models-and-pricing#cursor-models) and Composer) and third-party (API) plan usage from Cursor's `GetCurrentPeriodUsage` endpoint and cache the result for sixty seconds. [Auto](https://cursor.com/docs/models-and-pricing#auto-modes) is a router with Cost, Balance, and Intelligence modes that bill whichever model they pick, so a stretch of Auto can fill either bar.

| Slot | Claude Code | Cursor CLI |
|---|---|---|
| Model | yes | yes |
| Context bar | yes | yes |
| Session cost | yes | no |
| 5-hour / 7-day rate | yes | no |
| First-party / third-party plan | no | yes |
| Repo / branch | yes | yes |

You need `bash`, [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/), and `git`. Cursor's plan bars also need `curl` and a signed-in CLI. The bars use 24-bit RGB, so a [truecolor terminal](https://github.com/termstandard/colors) is the difference between a gradient and a muddle.

## The Key Is `statusLine`

The wiring is a JSON object named `statusLine` - capital L. Claude Code reads it from [`~/.claude/settings.json`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline). Cursor CLI reads it from [`~/.cursor/cli-config.json`](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/reference/configuration). Same shape: `"type": "command"` and a `command` path. Merge that object into the file you already have. Do not replace the rest of the file. If `CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR` or `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, Cursor may be reading a different `cli-config.json`; merge into the file the running CLI actually uses.

Claude Code's block:

```json
{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh"
  }
}
```

Cursor CLI's block, including the `padding: 2` I actually run:

```json
{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.cursor/statusline.sh",
    "padding": 2
  }
}
```

That is the whole difference in setup. The scripts below assume those paths: `~/.claude/statusline.sh` and `~/.cursor/statusline.sh`.

## GNU `stat` Is Not BSD `stat`

Claude's script never asks `stat` for a file's mtime, so the Linux copy and the macOS copy are the same file.

Cursor's plan bars cache for sixty seconds, and the Linux copy used [GNU `stat -c %Y`](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/stat-invocation.html). macOS ships [BSD `stat`](https://ss64.com/mac/stat.html), which wants `stat -f %m`. GNU syntax on a Mac fails, the cache looks stale on every paint, and you refetch more than you meant to.

The macOS script tries GNU first and falls back to BSD:

```bash
mtime=$(stat -c %Y "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || stat -f %m "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
```

The other hole is the token. On Linux, Cursor CLI leaves an access token in `~/.config/cursor/auth.json`. On macOS it puts the same secret in Keychain (`cursor-access-token` / `cursor-user`) and often never writes that file. The Linux script reads the file and gives up. The macOS script tries the file, then Keychain.

Take the GNU script on Linux. Take the BSD script on macOS. The BSD script also runs on Linux - GNU `stat` succeeds on the first try, and the Keychain branch is skipped - but both copies are below so an agent does not have to guess.

The two Cursor scripts differ only in how they read the token and how they call `stat`.

## Steal Them

If you are an agent installing this for a human: pick the harness they are in. Claude Code gets the `statusLine` block for `~/.claude/settings.json` plus the Claude script, saved as `~/.claude/statusline.sh`. Cursor CLI gets the `statusLine` block for `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` plus the GNU script on Linux / WSL or the BSD script on macOS, saved as `~/.cursor/statusline.sh`. Mark the script executable. Merge the JSON object named `statusLine` (capital L). Do not overwrite the rest of the config file.

If you are a human: paste this post at an agent and say which prompt you live in. Or copy the matching fences yourself.

1. Save the script to the path in the heading.
2. `chmod +x` that path.
3. Merge the matching `statusLine` object.
4. Restart the CLI session.

### Claude Code: merge into `~/.claude/settings.json`

```json
{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh"
  }
}
```

### Claude Code: `~/.claude/statusline.sh` (macOS and Linux)

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claude Code status line: RGB gradient, dynamic emoji, cost, code velocity

input=$(cat)

# ── Colors ──
CYAN='\033[36m'
GREEN='\033[32m'
YELLOW='\033[33m'
RED='\033[31m'
MAGENTA='\033[35m'
DIM='\033[2m'
BOLD='\033[1m'
RESET='\033[0m'

BAR_WIDTH=15

# ── Truecolor helper ──
rgb() { printf '\033[38;2;%d;%d;%dm' "$1" "$2" "$3"; }

# ── Parse JSON fields ──
model=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.model.display_name // "Unknown"')
used=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.context_window.used_percentage // empty')
cost=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.cost.total_cost_usd // 0')
rate_5h=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.rate_limits.five_hour.used_percentage // empty')
rate_7d=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.rate_limits.seven_day.used_percentage // empty')
cwd=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.workspace.current_dir // .cwd // ""')

# ── Git info ──
branch=""
repo=""
if [ -n "$cwd" ]; then
  branch=$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null)
  repo=$(basename "$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)" 2>/dev/null)
fi

# ── Bar drawing helper ──
draw_bar() {
  local pct=$1 grad_low_r=$2 grad_low_g=$3 grad_low_b=$4 grad_high_r=$5 grad_high_g=$6 grad_high_b=$7
  local pct_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$pct")
  local filled=$(( (pct_int * BAR_WIDTH + 50) / 100 ))
  local bar=""

  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    local pos=$(( i * 100 / (BAR_WIDTH - 1) ))
    local r=$(( grad_low_r + (grad_high_r - grad_low_r) * pos / 100 ))
    local g=$(( grad_low_g + (grad_high_g - grad_low_g) * pos / 100 ))
    local b=$(( grad_low_b + (grad_high_b - grad_low_b) * pos / 100 ))

    if [ "$i" -lt "$filled" ]; then
      bar="${bar}$(rgb $r $g $b)█"
    else
      bar="${bar}\033[38;2;60;60;60m░"
    fi
  done
  printf '%b' "${bar}${RESET}"
}

# ── Context bar: green→yellow→red ──
if [ -n "$used" ]; then
  used_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$used")

  ctx_bar=$(draw_bar "$used_int" 0 200 80 220 20 0)

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then status_emoji="🚨"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then status_emoji="🔥"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 20 ]; then status_emoji="⚡"
  else status_emoji="🟢"; fi

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_color="$GREEN"; fi

  ctx_part="${status_emoji} ${ctx_bar} ${pct_color}${used_int}%${RESET}"
else
  empty_bar=""
  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    empty_bar="${empty_bar}░"
  done
  ctx_part="🟢 \033[38;2;60;60;60m${empty_bar}${RESET} --%"
fi

# ── Rate limit bars: red and purple gradients ──
rate_bars=""
if [ -n "$rate_5h" ]; then
  rate_5h_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$rate_5h")
  rate_5h_bar=$(draw_bar "$rate_5h_int" 150 50 50 220 0 0)

  if [ "$rate_5h_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_5h_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$rate_5h_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_5h_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_5h_color="$GREEN"; fi

  rate_bars="🕐 ${rate_5h_bar} ${pct_5h_color}${rate_5h_int}%${RESET}"
fi
if [ -n "$rate_7d" ]; then
  rate_7d_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$rate_7d")
  rate_7d_bar=$(draw_bar "$rate_7d_int" 150 80 150 220 80 220)

  if [ "$rate_7d_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_7d_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$rate_7d_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_7d_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_7d_color="$GREEN"; fi

  rate_bars="${rate_bars:+$rate_bars }📅 ${rate_7d_bar} ${pct_7d_color}${rate_7d_int}%${RESET}"
fi

# ── Cost ──
cost_part="${YELLOW}$(printf '$%.2f' "$cost")${RESET}"

# ── Single line: model | context | cost | rate limits | repo/branch ──
out="${MAGENTA}🤖 ${model}${RESET}"
out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${ctx_part}"
out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${cost_part}"
[ -n "$rate_bars" ] && out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${rate_bars}"

# Add repo/branch at the end if present
if [ -n "$repo" ] || [ -n "$branch" ]; then
  out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET}"
  [ -n "$repo" ] && out="${out} ${BOLD}${YELLOW}${repo}${RESET}"
  [ -n "$branch" ] && out="${out}${repo:+ }${BOLD}${CYAN}🌿 (${branch})${RESET}"
fi

printf '%b' "$out"
```

### Cursor CLI: merge into `~/.cursor/cli-config.json`

```json
{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.cursor/statusline.sh",
    "padding": 2
  }
}
```

### Cursor CLI: `~/.cursor/statusline.sh` on GNU / Linux

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cursor CLI status line — port of ~/.claude/statusline.sh
# 5h/7d rate bars → first-party (auto/composer) / third-party (API) plan usage

input=$(cat)

# ── Colors ──
CYAN='\033[36m'
GREEN='\033[32m'
YELLOW='\033[33m'
RED='\033[31m'
MAGENTA='\033[35m'
DIM='\033[2m'
BOLD='\033[1m'
RESET='\033[0m'

BAR_WIDTH=15

# ── Truecolor helper ──
rgb() { printf '\033[38;2;%d;%d;%dm' "$1" "$2" "$3"; }

# ── Parse JSON fields from statusline payload ──
model=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.model.display_name // "Unknown"')
used=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.context_window.used_percentage // empty')
cwd=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.workspace.current_dir // .cwd // ""')
# Prefer payload fields if Cursor ever ships them; else filled from usage cache below
fp_pct=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.usage.auto_percent_used // .usage.autoPercentUsed // .planUsage.autoPercentUsed // empty')
tp_pct=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.usage.api_percent_used // .usage.apiPercentUsed // .planUsage.apiPercentUsed // empty')

# ── Cached GetCurrentPeriodUsage (first-/third-party plan bars) ──
# No session cost in Cursor's statusline payload or usage API — dollar slot omitted.
CACHE_FILE="${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/cursor-statusline-usage.json"
CACHE_TTL_SEC=60
AUTH_FILE="${CURSOR_AUTH_FILE:-$HOME/.config/cursor/auth.json}"

refresh_usage_cache() {
  local token
  token=$(jq -r '.accessToken // empty' "$AUTH_FILE" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
  [ -n "$token" ] || return 1
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$CACHE_FILE")" 2>/dev/null || true
  local tmp
  tmp=$(mktemp "${CACHE_FILE}.XXXXXX" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
  if curl -sS --max-time 1.5 \
      -X POST 'https://api2.cursor.sh/aiserver.v1.DashboardService/GetCurrentPeriodUsage' \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H 'Connect-Protocol-Version: 1' \
      -d '{}' \
      -o "$tmp" 2>/dev/null \
    && jq -e '.planUsage' "$tmp" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    mv -f "$tmp" "$CACHE_FILE"
    return 0
  fi
  rm -f "$tmp"
  return 1
}

cache_fresh() {
  [ -f "$CACHE_FILE" ] || return 1
  local age mtime now
  mtime=$(stat -c %Y "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
  now=$(date +%s)
  age=$((now - mtime))
  [ "$age" -lt "$CACHE_TTL_SEC" ]
}

if ! cache_fresh; then
  refresh_usage_cache || true
fi

if [ -f "$CACHE_FILE" ]; then
  [ -z "$fp_pct" ] && fp_pct=$(jq -r '.planUsage.autoPercentUsed // empty' "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
  [ -z "$tp_pct" ] && tp_pct=$(jq -r '.planUsage.apiPercentUsed // empty' "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
fi

# ── Git info ──
branch=""
repo=""
if [ -n "$cwd" ]; then
  branch=$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null)
  repo=$(basename "$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)" 2>/dev/null)
fi

# ── Bar drawing helper ──
draw_bar() {
  local pct=$1 grad_low_r=$2 grad_low_g=$3 grad_low_b=$4 grad_high_r=$5 grad_high_g=$6 grad_high_b=$7
  local pct_int
  pct_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$pct")
  local filled=$(( (pct_int * BAR_WIDTH + 50) / 100 ))
  [ "$filled" -gt "$BAR_WIDTH" ] && filled=$BAR_WIDTH
  [ "$filled" -lt 0 ] && filled=0
  local bar=""

  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    local pos=$(( i * 100 / (BAR_WIDTH - 1) ))
    local r=$(( grad_low_r + (grad_high_r - grad_low_r) * pos / 100 ))
    local g=$(( grad_low_g + (grad_high_g - grad_low_g) * pos / 100 ))
    local b=$(( grad_low_b + (grad_high_b - grad_low_b) * pos / 100 ))

    if [ "$i" -lt "$filled" ]; then
      bar="${bar}$(rgb $r $g $b)█"
    else
      bar="${bar}\033[38;2;60;60;60m░"
    fi
  done
  printf '%b' "${bar}${RESET}"
}

# ── Context bar: green→yellow→red ──
if [ -n "$used" ]; then
  used_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$used")

  ctx_bar=$(draw_bar "$used_int" 0 200 80 220 20 0)

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then status_emoji="🚨"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then status_emoji="🔥"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 20 ]; then status_emoji="⚡"
  else status_emoji="🟢"; fi

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_color="$GREEN"; fi

  ctx_part="${status_emoji} ${ctx_bar} ${pct_color}${used_int}%${RESET}"
else
  empty_bar=""
  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    empty_bar="${empty_bar}░"
  done
  ctx_part="🟢 \033[38;2;60;60;60m${empty_bar}${RESET} --%"
fi

# ── First-party (auto/composer) + third-party (API) bars ──
usage_bars=""
if [ -n "$fp_pct" ]; then
  fp_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$fp_pct")
  fp_bar=$(draw_bar "$fp_int" 150 50 50 220 0 0)

  if [ "$fp_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_fp_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$fp_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_fp_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_fp_color="$GREEN"; fi

  usage_bars="🏠 ${fp_bar} ${pct_fp_color}${fp_int}%${RESET}"
fi
if [ -n "$tp_pct" ]; then
  tp_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$tp_pct")
  tp_bar=$(draw_bar "$tp_int" 150 80 150 220 80 220)

  if [ "$tp_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_tp_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$tp_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_tp_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_tp_color="$GREEN"; fi

  usage_bars="${usage_bars:+$usage_bars }🌐 ${tp_bar} ${pct_tp_color}${tp_int}%${RESET}"
fi

# ── Single line: model | context | 1P/3P usage | repo/branch ──
out="${MAGENTA}🤖 ${model}${RESET}"
out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${ctx_part}"
[ -n "$usage_bars" ] && out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${usage_bars}"

if [ -n "$repo" ] || [ -n "$branch" ]; then
  out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET}"
  [ -n "$repo" ] && out="${out} ${BOLD}${YELLOW}${repo}${RESET}"
  [ -n "$branch" ] && out="${out}${repo:+ }${BOLD}${CYAN}🌿 (${branch})${RESET}"
fi

printf '%b' "$out"
```

### Cursor CLI: `~/.cursor/statusline.sh` on macOS / BSD

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cursor CLI status line — port of ~/.claude/statusline.sh
# 5h/7d rate bars → first-party (auto/composer) / third-party (API) plan usage

input=$(cat)

# ── Colors ──
CYAN='\033[36m'
GREEN='\033[32m'
YELLOW='\033[33m'
RED='\033[31m'
MAGENTA='\033[35m'
DIM='\033[2m'
BOLD='\033[1m'
RESET='\033[0m'

BAR_WIDTH=15

# ── Truecolor helper ──
rgb() { printf '\033[38;2;%d;%d;%dm' "$1" "$2" "$3"; }

# ── Parse JSON fields from statusline payload ──
model=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.model.display_name // "Unknown"')
used=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.context_window.used_percentage // empty')
cwd=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.workspace.current_dir // .cwd // ""')
# Prefer payload fields if Cursor ever ships them; else filled from usage cache below
fp_pct=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.usage.auto_percent_used // .usage.autoPercentUsed // .planUsage.autoPercentUsed // empty')
tp_pct=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.usage.api_percent_used // .usage.apiPercentUsed // .planUsage.apiPercentUsed // empty')

# ── Cached GetCurrentPeriodUsage (first-/third-party plan bars) ──
# No session cost in Cursor's statusline payload or usage API — dollar slot omitted.
CACHE_FILE="${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/cursor-statusline-usage.json"
CACHE_TTL_SEC=60
AUTH_FILE="${CURSOR_AUTH_FILE:-$HOME/.config/cursor/auth.json}"
AUTH_FILE_DARWIN="${HOME}/.cursor/auth.json"

get_access_token() {
  local token f
  for f in "$AUTH_FILE" "$AUTH_FILE_DARWIN"; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    token=$(jq -r '.accessToken // empty' "$f" 2>/dev/null) || continue
    [ -n "$token" ] && { printf '%s' "$token"; return 0; }
  done
  if [ "$(uname -s)" = "Darwin" ] && command -v security >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    token=$(security find-generic-password -s cursor-access-token -a cursor-user -w 2>/dev/null) || true
    [ -n "$token" ] && { printf '%s' "$token"; return 0; }
  fi
  return 1
}

refresh_usage_cache() {
  local token
  token=$(get_access_token) || return 1
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$CACHE_FILE")" 2>/dev/null || true
  local tmp
  tmp=$(mktemp "${CACHE_FILE}.XXXXXX" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
  if curl -sS --max-time 1.5 \
      -X POST 'https://api2.cursor.sh/aiserver.v1.DashboardService/GetCurrentPeriodUsage' \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${token}" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H 'Connect-Protocol-Version: 1' \
      -d '{}' \
      -o "$tmp" 2>/dev/null \
    && jq -e '.planUsage' "$tmp" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    mv -f "$tmp" "$CACHE_FILE"
    return 0
  fi
  rm -f "$tmp"
  return 1
}

cache_fresh() {
  [ -f "$CACHE_FILE" ] || return 1
  local age mtime now
  mtime=$(stat -c %Y "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || stat -f %m "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
  now=$(date +%s)
  age=$((now - mtime))
  [ "$age" -lt "$CACHE_TTL_SEC" ]
}

if ! cache_fresh; then
  refresh_usage_cache || true
fi

if [ -f "$CACHE_FILE" ]; then
  [ -z "$fp_pct" ] && fp_pct=$(jq -r '.planUsage.autoPercentUsed // empty' "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
  [ -z "$tp_pct" ] && tp_pct=$(jq -r '.planUsage.apiPercentUsed // empty' "$CACHE_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
fi

# ── Git info ──
branch=""
repo=""
if [ -n "$cwd" ]; then
  branch=$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null)
  repo=$(basename "$(git -C "$cwd" --no-optional-locks rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)" 2>/dev/null)
fi

# ── Bar drawing helper ──
draw_bar() {
  local pct=$1 grad_low_r=$2 grad_low_g=$3 grad_low_b=$4 grad_high_r=$5 grad_high_g=$6 grad_high_b=$7
  local pct_int
  pct_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$pct")
  local filled=$(( (pct_int * BAR_WIDTH + 50) / 100 ))
  [ "$filled" -gt "$BAR_WIDTH" ] && filled=$BAR_WIDTH
  [ "$filled" -lt 0 ] && filled=0
  local bar=""

  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    local pos=$(( i * 100 / (BAR_WIDTH - 1) ))
    local r=$(( grad_low_r + (grad_high_r - grad_low_r) * pos / 100 ))
    local g=$(( grad_low_g + (grad_high_g - grad_low_g) * pos / 100 ))
    local b=$(( grad_low_b + (grad_high_b - grad_low_b) * pos / 100 ))

    if [ "$i" -lt "$filled" ]; then
      bar="${bar}$(rgb $r $g $b)█"
    else
      bar="${bar}\033[38;2;60;60;60m░"
    fi
  done
  printf '%b' "${bar}${RESET}"
}

# ── Context bar: green→yellow→red ──
if [ -n "$used" ]; then
  used_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$used")

  ctx_bar=$(draw_bar "$used_int" 0 200 80 220 20 0)

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then status_emoji="🚨"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then status_emoji="🔥"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 20 ]; then status_emoji="⚡"
  else status_emoji="🟢"; fi

  if [ "$used_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$used_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_color="$GREEN"; fi

  ctx_part="${status_emoji} ${ctx_bar} ${pct_color}${used_int}%${RESET}"
else
  empty_bar=""
  for (( i=0; i<BAR_WIDTH; i++ )); do
    empty_bar="${empty_bar}░"
  done
  ctx_part="🟢 \033[38;2;60;60;60m${empty_bar}${RESET} --%"
fi

# ── First-party (auto/composer) + third-party (API) bars ──
usage_bars=""
if [ -n "$fp_pct" ]; then
  fp_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$fp_pct")
  fp_bar=$(draw_bar "$fp_int" 150 50 50 220 0 0)

  if [ "$fp_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_fp_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$fp_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_fp_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_fp_color="$GREEN"; fi

  usage_bars="🏠 ${fp_bar} ${pct_fp_color}${fp_int}%${RESET}"
fi
if [ -n "$tp_pct" ]; then
  tp_int=$(printf '%.0f' "$tp_pct")
  tp_bar=$(draw_bar "$tp_int" 150 80 150 220 80 220)

  if [ "$tp_int" -ge 90 ]; then pct_tp_color="$RED"
  elif [ "$tp_int" -ge 70 ]; then pct_tp_color="$YELLOW"
  else pct_tp_color="$GREEN"; fi

  usage_bars="${usage_bars:+$usage_bars }🌐 ${tp_bar} ${pct_tp_color}${tp_int}%${RESET}"
fi

# ── Single line: model | context | 1P/3P usage | repo/branch ──
out="${MAGENTA}🤖 ${model}${RESET}"
out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${ctx_part}"
[ -n "$usage_bars" ] && out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET} ${usage_bars}"

if [ -n "$repo" ] || [ -n "$branch" ]; then
  out="${out} ${DIM}|${RESET}"
  [ -n "$repo" ] && out="${out} ${BOLD}${YELLOW}${repo}${RESET}"
  [ -n "$branch" ] && out="${out}${repo:+ }${BOLD}${CYAN}🌿 (${branch})${RESET}"
fi

printf '%b' "$out"
```

## Stockroom: Find the Conversation You Half-Remember

Earlier today I needed a conversation from mid-July. Not by id - by meaning. Something about "blogging about stockroom," asked from [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/), about a [Cursor](https://cursor.com/) session I only half-remembered.

Stockroom's [search](https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/user-guide/search/) put that Cursor session at rank one. The retrieved plan became the plan for this post.

That is the whole pitch. Your agents have been writing history to disk the whole time. I built [Stockroom](https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/) so you can ask about it - from either harness, about either harness - without hoping the vendor's UI still has the thread.

**[Stockroom 1.0 is out.](https://github.com/Texarkanine/stockroom)**

## Your Transcripts, One Warehouse

One local [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) file. Full prompts, responses, and tool inputs - kept whole. Truncation is a read-time convenience, never a storage-time loss.

Two ways in:

- **Ask the agent.** Slash-invoke `/sr-search` (Claude: `/stockroom:sr-search`) and let it pick SQL, meaning search, or both. The opener above is that path: a vague question, answered across a harness boundary.
- **Skip the agent.** After setup, `stockroom query` and the local [dashboard](https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/user-guide/dashboard/) work offline. No cloud index of your coding sessions.

<div class="polaroid-container">

      <img src="stockroom-dashboard-top-light.png" alt="Stockroom local dashboard showing session history across harnesses" width="600" class="polaroid-image">
    </a>
    <div class="polaroid-title">Stockroom dashboard</div>

      (<a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20260812011108/https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/user-guide/dashboard/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">archive</a>)
      
    </small>
  </div>
</div>


**It backfills.** Harness formats come and go; Stockroom reads what is still on disk, including formats the vendors already abandoned. On this machine the warehouse holds a bit over 113,000 messages across Cursor and Claude Code, reaching back to September 2025 - months before Stockroom's first commit in June 2026. The cameras were running. Stockroom just lets you re-watch the tapes.

That "pays backwards" feeling is what [Just Try the Thing](/2026/08/01/just-try-the-thing.html) was pointing at: agents can use work from *before* the warehouse existed, because the raw logs were already on disk. [Disintegration of Persistence of Memory.md](/2026/08/03/disintegration-of-persistence-of-memory-md.html) puts the same store on the memory ladder as rung five - security-camera footage for *how* and *why*, not a notepad you hope somebody kept tidy. Those posts argue the need. This one is the install.

Cursor and Claude Code share one schema. Every table already carries `harness` as a first-class column, so another ingest path later is additive - not a rewrite dressed up as a feature. I may add more harnesses; I may not. Day one already speaks two.

## From Zero to /sr-search

1. Add the [txrk9-agent-plugins](https://github.com/Texarkanine/txrk9-agent-plugins) marketplace, then install the `stockroom` plugin from it.
2. **Cursor only:** enable **Include third-party Plugins, Skills, and other configs** (Settings → Rules, Skills, Subagents). Plugin hooks do not register without it.
3. Run first-time setup:
   - Cursor: `/sr-initialize`
   - Claude Code: `/stockroom:sr-initialize`
4. Ask about past work, or slash-invoke search:

```text
/sr-search "What was the most-recent time I had to correct an agent's behavior?"
```

`sr-initialize` provisions the per-machine torch wheel (for meaning search), puts `stockroom` on your PATH, offers nightly ingest+embed, and runs the first full ingest. Re-runs are safe: it re-probes and only does what is still missing.

Full walkthrough, including what landed on disk and what to try next: the [Quickstart](https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/user-guide/quickstart/).

## Open Source, Tagged 1.0.0

Stockroom is open source under AGPL-3.0 at [github.com/Texarkanine/stockroom](https://github.com/Texarkanine/stockroom). Docs live at [texarkanine.github.io/stockroom](https://texarkanine.github.io/stockroom/). [v1.0.0](https://github.com/Texarkanine/stockroom/releases/tag/v1.0.0) just shipped; the marketplace plugin path above pulls current.

If you half-remember a conversation and wish either agent could find it:

```text
/sr-search "blogging about stockroom"
```

Worst case, you learn what your warehouse does not have yet. Best case, last month answers.

## a16n: Take Your Agent Customization Anywhere

You've spent weeks tuning your AI coding agent. Rules for how it handles your React components. Skills for your deployment workflow. Ignore patterns so it stays out of generated code. Slash commands for common operations. It all works beautifully.

Then your team gets Claude Code licenses. Or you want to try Cursor on a side project. Or half your team uses one tool and half uses the other.

Your choices: re-create everything by hand, or lose it.

I built [a16n](https://github.com/Texarkanine/a16n) so neither has to happen.

## What It Does

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude
```

That reads your Cursor rules, skills, commands, and ignore patterns, and writes equivalent Claude Code configuration. The reverse works too:

```bash
npx a16n convert --from claude --to cursor
```

Your carefully-crafted agent setup comes with you. One command, both directions.

## Getting Started

No install required. `npx` handles it:

```bash
# See what you have (without changing anything)
npx a16n discover --from cursor

# Preview the conversion
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --dry-run

# Do it for real
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude
```

That's the whole recipe. Three commands: inspect, preview, convert.

If you want it permanently:

```bash
npm install -g a16n
```

## What Converts

a16n understands six kinds of agent customization:

| What | Cursor | Claude Code |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **Global prompts** | `alwaysApply: true` rules | `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md` |
| **File rules** | `globs: [...]` rules | `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` |
| **Skills** | Rules with `description:`, `.cursor/skills/` | `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` |
| **Manual prompts** | `.cursor/commands/*.md` | Skills with `disable-model-invocation` |
| **Ignore patterns** | `.cursorignore` | `permissions.deny` |
| **Full skill packages** | [AgentSkills.io](https://agentskills.io) format | AgentSkills.io format |

Things that translate cleanly just translate. Things that can't (like Claude's hooks, or Cursor commands that use `$ARGUMENTS`) get skipped with a clear warning telling you why. No silent data loss.

## Beyond Two Tools

a16n isn't hardwired to Cursor and Claude. It uses a plugin architecture: each tool is a plugin that knows how to read and write its own format. Cursor and Claude are built in. More can be added.

There's also a neutral format - the a16n IR - that you can convert to and from:

```bash
# Store your config in a tool-agnostic format
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to a16n

# Render it for any supported tool
npx a16n convert --from a16n --to claude
```

This makes a16n useful as a hub. Maintain one canonical set of agent customization and generate tool-specific configuration on demand - per developer, per project, per CI run.

Third-party plugins are auto-discovered from npm. If a package is named `a16n-plugin-*` and implements the plugin interface, `a16n` will find it. There's already one: [a16n-plugin-cursorrules](https://www.npmjs.com/package/a16n-plugin-cursorrules) adds support for the legacy `.cursorrules` format:

```bash
npm install -g a16n-plugin-cursorrules
npx a16n convert --from cursorrules --to cursor
```

## Useful Flags

A few things that came up during real use:

**Separate read/write directories.** Read from one project, write to another:

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --from-dir ./proj-a --to-dir ./proj-b
```

**Path reference rewriting.** If your rule content references file paths (like `.cursor/rules/auth.mdc`), a16n can rewrite those references to point to the new locations:

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --rewrite-path-refs
```

**Source cleanup.** Delete the source files after conversion (only if they were fully consumed - partially-converted sources are preserved):

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --delete-source
```

**Git integration.** Control whether output files are tracked or ignored:

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --gitignore-output-with match
```

## The Name

a16n is a numeronym, like i18n (internationalization) or l10n (localization). Smash "agent customization" together and count the letters between the first and last: a-[gentcustomizatio]-n. Sixteen. It's short, it's `npm`-able, and it was available.

## Status

a16n is [on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/a16n) at v0.13.0. I've been running it in my own workflow for a couple of weeks without incident. The [documentation](https://texarkanine.github.io/a16n/) covers the CLI, conversion semantics, and plugin development.

It's open source under AGPL-3.0 at [github.com/Texarkanine/a16n](https://github.com/Texarkanine/a16n). Contributions welcome - especially plugins for tools I don't use. If you're curious about how it got built, there's a [companion diary](/2026/03/13/seven-weeks.html).

If you have agent customization in one tool and wish you had it in another, give it a try:

```bash
npx a16n convert --from cursor --to claude --dry-run
```

The worst that happens is you see what would change.
